Management Plan
2026
JOINT RESEARCH CENTRE
1

PART 1. Introduction
The Joint Research Centre (JRC) provides independent, evidence-based knowledge and science,
supporting European Union policies to positively impact society. It contributes to EU policymaking
in a variety of key areas such as agriculture and food security, digital transition and nuclear
safety. The JRC differs from a typical Commission Directorate-General regarding:
- governance: the JRC has a Board of Governors made up of national representatives;
- geographical presence: its research infrastructures are spread over six sites in five
different Member States;
- site management: the JRC is responsible for the full management of its sites
(infrastructure including laboratories, logistics, health and safety, environment, security).
The mutual rights and responsibilities with the host Member States are set out in site
agreements with the Commission;
- quality certifications: the JRC’s Integrated Management System is certified according
to the quality system ISO 9001, providing the framework for standards covering also
health and safety and environment.
Strategic planning and programming is the cornerstone of the Commission’s performance
management framework. The Commission’s strategic plan for 2025-2029 translates the
political priorities set in the Political Guidelines of President von der Leyen into general objectives.
This process ensures institutional coherence, enhances accountability, and aligns the actions of
all Commission services with the strategic vision of the mandate.
Within this framework, each Commission service has developed a strategic outlook for 2025-
2029 (see JRC 2025 management plan). This outlook defines a set of multiannual objectives
and indicators to measure progress towards their achievement. These will be used for planning
and reporting on performance throughout the period.
The 2026 management plan sets out what the JRC intends to deliver this year to contribute to
these multiannual objectives (part 2). It also describes how the JRC will contribute to the common
objective of building a modern and sustainable public administration (part 3). The main outputs
with their indicators and targets are presented in Annexes 1 and 2.

PART 2. Delivering on the Commission’s
priorities in 2026
Commission General Objective 8: A modern, high-performing and sustainable European
Commission
Specific Objective 8.1: The JRC supports evidence-informed policymaking through
creating and managing high-quality and fit-for-purpose scientific knowledge
In 2025, the Commission approved the JRC work programme for years 2025-2027 (1). The JRC
work programme is prepared together with other Directorates-General, is aligned with the
Commission political priorities and the JRC is determined to implement it in the upcoming years.
Specifically, in 2026, JRC will contribute to all seven of the Commission’s political priorities:
• 28th Regime for Innovative Companies – the JRC will provide support to the impact
assessment and will help to assess the macro impact of the initiative.
• European Innovation Agenda – the JRC will evaluate the economic effects of the
simplifications proposed by the European Innovation Act and carry out a literature review
on regulatory sandboxes included in the Act.
• Public Procurement Act – together with DG GROW, the JRC will prepare a case study
on steel in the construction sector. It will also provide economic modelling based on its
modelling and green requirements setting expertise, evaluating the cost of “buy
European”.
• Circular Economy Act – the JRC will support DG ENV in preparation of the Act’s impact
assessment. It will also contribute to the review of the Waste Electronic and Electronic
Equipment Directive, notably on recovery of Critical Raw Materials.
• Energy – The JRC will employ its modelling tools and provide scientific analysis to support
the Electrification Action Plan, the Energy Union governance update, the development of
CO2 transportation infrastructure, energy efficiency and renewable energy frameworks.
• European integrated framework for climate resilience – the JRC expects to provide
an analysis of the economic consequences at regional level, assessing the impact on long-
term macroeconomic asymmetries within EU regions.
• Biotech Act I – to support the Act’s implementation, the JRC will work on new genomic
techniques and gene editing, and on biotechnologies, including by operating several key
laboratories, patents analysis and market assessment.
• Advanced Materials Act – The JRC will provide scientific evidence, focusing on key
sectors (e.g., energy, construction, mobility), energy transition and certified reference

materials. With RTD, the JRC will identify research for critical raw material dependencies
reduction and make results accessible through the Raw Materials Information System.
• In 2026 (2) the JRC aims to carry out work on defence data gaps. It will draw up a
repository of JRC defence-relevant work to map gaps in its work in the field.
• JRC will contribute to preparing the annual report on the single EU defence market.
• The JRC will also test the added value of deeper cooperation with the European
Defence Agency and contribute to the defence readiness roadmap 2030 and
defence transformation roadmap.
• The JRC will inaugurate a Security Research and Innovation Campus, as stated in the
ProtectEU Internal Security Strategy, to bring our research in the security domain
closer to the operational agencies and member states.
• Construction Services Act – the JRC aims to contribute to the initiative on resilience of
the built environment, EUROCODES or the New European Bauhaus.
• Strategy for outermost regions – the JRC is cooperating with DG REGIO to analyse
renewable potential in EU regions, including in the outermost regions.
• Communication on island and coastal communities – through the EU blue economy
observatory, the JRC, together with DG MARE, plans to contribute to this communication,
for example with regards to coastal resilience.
• Anti-poverty strategy – the JRC will carry out an analysis on the impact on poverty
from a dynamic, life-course perspective of minimum income schemes, minimum wages,
increased employment and skill changes.
• Initiative on short-term rentals – building on its ample work on housing, the JRC will
focus on the role of tourism and short-term rentals and carry out a causality analysis of
short-term rentals on house prices.
• European strategy on sustainable tourism – the tourism dashboard developed by
the JRC provides the basis for forthcoming analyses relating to residents' perception of
tourism as well as the total economic impact of tourism in EU Member States' GDP.
• Cardiovascular health plan – the JRC will contribute with expertise in disease
prevention and health promotion, trustworthiness and uptake of AI in health, and by
enhancing the human relevance of cardiovascular research.
(2) In the field of defence and security, the JRC will only act within the mandate provided by its funding
programmes.
6

• Livestock strategy, including elements on animal welfare – the JRC will support
the strategy by providing scientific evidence on livestock feeding techniques effects on
climate, environment and production outcomes, as well as provide one or two models to
run livestock-specific scenarios.
• Rules on unfair trading practices in the food chain – the JRC is ready to conduct
surveys on the presence of the unfair trading practices in the EU food supply chain.
• Ocean Act – the JRC will support the development and implementation of the Ocean Act
through its work on the EU blue economy and the marine ecosystem. The JRC is well
placed to contribute to this area through its scientific advice provision to the common
fisheries policy and the marine strategy framework directive.
• Digital Fairness Act – the JRC will support DG JUST in the Act’s impact assessment by
participating in the evaluation of proposals for study contractors and by supporting the
contractors throughout the study.
• Anti-corruption strategy – the JRC’s e-platform for monitoring and tracking records of
court cases on organised crime and corruption in enlargement countries can contribute to
this initiative.
• Gender equality strategy 2026-2030 – the JRC will continue monitoring the state of
equality in the EU across six equality domains, including gender.
The JRC will also support evidence-informed policymaking through its horizontal work.
Even though the JRC is not a policy Directorate-General, it will support numerous simplification
efforts and implementation activities in other Directorates-General. For instance:
• In 2026, the JRC will collaborate with other DGs to develop a consolidated
Commission carbon accounting reference database and create a methodology to
reconcile national GHG inventories in agriculture with CAP mitigation assessments. The
JRC also provides data and models to the Carbon Farming database to support the Carbon
Removal framework. It will explore further collaboration with other DGs regarding carbon
accounting simplification and harmonisation, especially on aligning the Environmental
Footprint recommendation to the way forward suggested by relevant working groups and
on further developing a potential way ahead for carbon data management.
• The JRC will explore the practical policy use of the Commission’s sustainable and
inclusive wellbeing dashboard, for example, in the context of impact assessment and
multiannual financial framework monitoring, and of the EU’s involvement in the initiatives
following up the UN Summit for the Future.
• In 2026, the JRC will collaborate with DG ENV to prepare two policy briefs on how Earth
observation can support and simplify reporting requirements for the water quality/water
7

resilience strategy and habitat mapping under the Nature Restoration Law and the EU
Deforestation-free Regulation.
• On transport, the JRC will support initiatives outlined in the automotive action plan,
aimed at simplifying practices related to vehicle type-approval and the deployment of
advanced vehicle systems. Additionally, the JRC will continue advancing the development
and operation of information systems and methods that simplify and expedite vehicle
certification and verification processes, with the potential to set global standards.
• In agriculture, the JRC is supporting the development of a European data
interoperability framework for agriculture. It will work closely with DG AGRI to
reduce the data collection and reporting burden on farmers and Member State
administrations by better integrating diverse data flows.
• 2026 will see a streamlining exercise intended to centralise nuclear material at JRC
sites, aiming to reduce the number of JRC sites with nuclear materials from 3 (Karlsruhe,
Geel, Ispra) to 2 (Karlsruhe and Geel).
• The JRC will support the development of a guidance document for the implementation
of the do no significant harm principle in the next Multiannual Financial Framework.
• The JRC will organise an implementation dialogue on demography for
Commissioner Šuica. Together with DG RTD, it will also produce an Annual Report on
Simplification, Implementation, and Enforcement for Commissioner Zaharieva, as well as
contribute to this report for Commissioners Šuica and Micallef.
• In 2026, the JRC will conduct impact case studies on its research portfolios
supporting the Union transport and migration policies. It will continue the
development and testing of efficiency and effectiveness assessment methods to refine
its research portfolio and optimise its contribution to shape policies, through analysis of
scientific activities, resources used, outputs and their transfer to respective stakeholders.
• Through its foresight work, the JRC will support the 2026 Commission strategic
foresight report. Similarly in 2026, the JRC Scientific Committee will use foresight
methodologies to develop a long-term science outlook for the JRC.
• In 2026, the JRC Scientific Committee will publish it excellence report monitoring JRC
scientific performance, with recommendations improving its research environment.
• In the upcoming years, the JRC aims to become a leading example of an AI-empowered
organisation, building on its internal AI expertise, and data and ICT infrastructure to
further boost its scientific impact, policy support and administrative efficiency. To work
towards this goal, the JRC will in 2026 identify and prioritise AI use cases with the
potential to increase its productivity, quality and efficiency. The JRC will also invest in the
human-centric dimension of the AI transformation to ensure the JRC builds a safe AI
culture, by building a dedicated JRC AI community.
• In 2026, the JRC will continue to support other Commission services in line with the
President’s mission letters to College of Commissioners. With these letters stating
8

proposals must be evidence-based, the Joint Research Centre, as the Commission’s
internal scientific service, is well suited to support this work. Similarly, the JRC will
continue to work with the other EU institutions to ensure policy and legislation draw
on high quality science and analysis.
• In 2026, the JRC will also continue to strengthen its relations with Member States and
countries associated with the Horizon Europe programme. This will be achieved through
targeted outreach activities involving the JRC’s two strategic stakeholder networks - the
Board of Governors and the network of national contact points (NCPs). The JRC, including
its Scientific Committee, will hold information sessions with NCPs on JRC activities and
use existing tools to enhance cooperation (e.g., joint actions, working groups,
information sessions).
• Relations with Member States will be further strengthened through strategic outreach
conducted by JRC senior management. These will include official visits and high-level
meetings with key policymakers in relevant ministries and with the leaders of key
scientific institutions operating within Member States.
• The JRC will pursue its support to candidate countries and its engagement with
international partners, including from Horizon Europe-associated countries and with
multilateral organisations, maximising the impact of science for policy. The JRC will
further develop its cooperation with Ukraine, Moldova, Switzerland, Canada and Japan.
Regarding the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine in 2026, the JRC will notably:
• contribute to the EU response to the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine, for
example by generating maps and geospatial intelligence products;
• continue to support Ukraine’s EU accession and its adoption of the EU acquis;
• through the New European Bauhaus (NEB), support Ukraine's sustainable
reconstruction by establishing a NEB Academy Hub in the country while working with
Ukrainian partners to ensure the successful reconstruction of schools;
• continue developing strategies to maintain the functioning of the food supply
chain in the face of disruptions to agricultural production and infrastructure, including
transport and storage;
• involve Ukrainian representatives in the European Network of National Air Quality
Reference Laboratories and the Forum for Air Quality Modelling;
• support DG INTPA under the Instrument for Nuclear Safety Cooperation as part of the JRC
Task Force on Ukraine;
• coordinate a project on a laboratory for high-level Radwaste in the Chernobyl
exclusion zone;
• support smart specialisation strategy (S3) in Ukraine by providing remote
methodological training to regional S3 teams, with the aim of analysing the current
situation in terms of economic, innovation and scientific potential;
• provide technical input for the list of sanctions against the Russian Federation.
Regarding responding to crises and emergencies the JRC will furthermore:
9

• support the design of an EU comprehensive risks and threats assessment with
interdisciplinary research on emerging and existing risks the EU faces. Work on conflicts
and natural hazards will be combined with research on health threats, cybersecurity,
hybrid threats, climate change, including tipping points and digital sovereignty;
• support, through a risk data hub, the preparedness strategy including internal security
strategy, water resilience strategy, European Health Union, the joint white paper for
European defence readiness 2030 and climate adaptation plan;
• organise, through the Disaster Risk Management Knowledge Centre, a science-
based dialogue within the Commission for coherent policymaking;
• improve understanding of population and built-up areas’ exposure to disasters and crises
through updates on the Global Human Settlement Layer;
• support the design and implementation of the European Crisis Management
Platform. The JRC will take the lead in developing a cross-sectoral description of
concepts and categories in the field of crisis management, while working with the
different DGs and eliciting domain-specific descriptions from them;
• drive the evolution of the early warning and monitoring capabilities of the Copernicus
Emergency Management Service;
• produce knowledge and support the development of standards and guidelines to improve
the resilience of the built environment and dual-use transport infrastructure to
face crises, including the effects of climate change;
• carry out research on critical and strategic raw materials to support the design
of circular economy policies in specific sectors (e.g., batteries, vehicles), and improve
coherence, quality and accessibility of key research outcomes through its Raw Materials
Information System, energy security including nuclear safety and security aspects, food
security, societal resilience and foreign direct investment screening;
• bridge civilian and military preparedness and support space and defence through
technology foresight, and expand research on dependencies and vulnerabilities in
technologies of strategic interest;
• carry out a proficiency test for European laboratories monitoring radioactivity in
the environment;
• create advancing models and approaches to understand infection dynamics,
enhancing outbreak predictive capabilities and work on in-silico workflows for
pathogen detection, e.g., antimicrobial resistance, enabling data-driven responses.
Specific Objective 8.2: The JRC develops and operates modern, sustainable and open
research infrastructures
To support modern research infrastructures development and maintenance of, the JRC plans to:
• align with European research infrastructure roadmaps. High importance is
attached to the collaboration with the European Strategy Forum on Research
Infrastructures (ESFRI) and European Research Infrastructure Consortia (ERIC). The JRC
will establish at least four new associations with ESFRI Roadmap and ERIC Consortia by
the end of 2027, ensuring its research infrastructures are aligned with EU priorities;
• improve the energy performance of buildings. The JRC will complete the energy
audit of its non-residential buildings. Where the audit is completed, the legal maximum
10

energy performance threshold (10% reduction) (3) will be applied, where applicable, to
new maintenance and infrastructure development interventions;
• renovate and refurbish buildings. The JRC has developed a renovation plan and
following the completion of the energy audit of its non-residential buildings, the plan will
be updated with the aim to refurbish at least 3% of its building stock annually,
incorporating energy-efficient systems such as solar panels and sustainable materials.
To achieve these goals, the JRC will in 2026:
• collaborate with European research and technology organisations to stay up to
date with the latest technological advancements and best practices in research
infrastructure operation, access and development;
• develop agile and new ways of providing access to JRC research infrastructures
to industry, including SMEs, startups and scaleups, in connection with EU programmes
supporting innovation. Access will comprise an ecosystem of services including data,
regulation, technology transfer, patents and proof-of-concept in support to innovation;
• boost and strengthen collaboration among JRC Directorates and the infrastructure
management teams within the Site Operation Network (SON), working towards a
coordinated common decision-making process for small and medium investments.
The SON will support the decision-making process for major investments (buildings,
research infrastructures and flagship research infrastructures) by the Group of Site
Directors;
• follow the JRC Investment Plan for short and long-term planning and prioritisation to
improve energy efficiency and ageing of existing buildings, including research and
research enabling infrastructure.
Specific Objective 8.3: The Commission has appropriate capacity to manage
intellectual property rights and be compliant with the rules and regulations
In 2026, the JRC will continue to facilitate appropriate intellectual property management at the
Commission, working together with the intellectual property correspondents’ network and the
Legal Service. Specifically, it will review the established guiding principles and practices in
Communication to the Commission. (4) Additional work in this area will focus on the JRC’s
intellectual property management awareness-raising activities, promoting the EURECA (EU
intellectual property resource catalogue) intellectual property management platform, and
providing legal advice on matters related to intellectual property rights.
Commission General Objective 1: A new plan for Europe's sustainable prosperity and
competitiveness
Specific Objective 1.1: The JRC contributes to the safe, efficient, and sustainable
phase-out of nuclear facilities by decommissioning JRC sites at the end of their
lifecycle and supporting EU knowledge transfer on decommissioning practices
Decommissioning and waste management are an integral part of the life cycle of the JRC’s
nuclear research facilities. They fulfil the aim of returning the land used to a ‘green-field

(4) (C(2022) 1225 final).

status’. The JRC’s nuclear decommissioning and waste management programme has a
set of specific activities and projects with related objectives.
In 2026, progress at the Ispra site on three main work streams (nuclear material and waste
management, and decommissioning) will include:
• completing the first decommissioning phase in the hot cell facility, with the removal of
all the experimental cells;
• progressing on the dismantling of the old liquid effluent treatment facility STRRL (5);
• starting to retrieve bituminised drums once the safety authority approves the
corresponding operational plan;
• shipping the first batch of metal for melting;
• issuing the decommissioning licence for the heavy water moderated and cooled nuclear
(ESSOR) reactor;
• preparing fresh nuclear material for transfer to a third party, after approval of all
authorization steps; and
• publishing a call for tender for treatment/conditioning of radioactive liquid waste.
At the Karlsruhe site, activities will focus on the progressive dismantling of the remaining glove
boxes and the continued management of legacy waste, building on the preparatory and
characterisation work performed in previous years. In parallel, efforts will continue to update the
site decommissioning plan, ensuring its gradual alignment with state-of-the-art national and
international standards in nuclear decommissioning planning.
At the Petten site, activities will focus on the continued treatment and conditioning of historical
waste, ensuring progress on the liabilities inventory and waste route optimisation. In parallel, the
site will prepare the update, due in 2027, of the mandatory decommissioning plan of the High
Flux Reactor, integrating the conclusions of the 2025 strategic assessment of decommissioning
scenarios. On this basis, the preferred implementation model will be further examined in terms
of technical feasibility, contractual options, and governance arrangements in coordination with
national counterparts and the host organisations.
At the Geel site, in addition to continuing small-scale legacy waste management activities,
the focus will be on advancing the licence modification process and technical discussions with
the Belgian regulatory authority (FANC) to enable the effective dismantling of Building 010 and
its Annex 090.
In 2026, the JRC will increase the production and sharing of knowledge products (6) linked to
decommissioning and waste management. (7)

(6) Knowledge products are tangible outputs of prepared knowledge, such as documents, services, events and
media, that enable action by selected users. Knowledge products are one of the key outcomes of knowledge
management process since they convey knowledge in an actionable manner.
(7) These knowledge products cover e.g., the application of remotely operated equipment for cutting pipelines
in reactor sub-flow areas and removing radioactive sources from storage facilities, public awareness
approaches for nuclear decommissioning and radioactive waste management, incineration of radioactive

12

PART 3. A modern and sustainable public
administration: outputs in 2026
The internal control framework supports sound management and decision-making. In particular,
it ensures that risks to the achievement of objectives are addressed and reduced to acceptable
levels through cost-effective controls.
The JRC has established an internal control system tailored to its particular characteristics and
circumstances. The effective functioning of this internal control system will be assessed on an
ongoing basis throughout the year and will be subject to an annual assessment covering all
internal control principles.
A. Human resource management
The JRC aims to recruit, train, motivate and retain highly qualified staff, while promoting equal
opportunities and diversity. The JRC priorities follow-up on the 2023 Commission staff survey
and the JRC’s 2025-2027 equality workplan. Key initiatives for 2026, detailed in Annex 2, p. 26,
include:
• improving workforce planning, by implementing a new staff planning mechanism to
accelerate recruitment, and by managing the reserve lists of the EPSO competition for
scientific researchers;
• dedicated outreach work and specific programmes to host scientists;
• increasing geographical and gender balance, through targeted outreach efforts;
• a new local action plan addressing the results of the 2025 staff survey;
• improving staff’s professional development, by implementing a 2025-2027 Learning &
Development strategic framework;
• improving the scientific, technical, and policy-related skills integral to the JRC's mission
by offering more targeted training tailored to its specific areas of work;
• preparing and upskilling staff for emerging technologies such as AI, data analytics and
digital collaboration tools;
• strengthening support for managers and team leaders, helping them navigate the
complexities of leading in a hybrid, multidisciplinary and inclusive environment;
strengthening the work culture including in terms of diversity and inclusion, with a focus
on neurodiversity.
B. Digital transformation and data management
Digital transformation
The JRC remains committed to digital transformation. Senior and middle management, together
with the Digital Steering Committee, ICT and Cybersecurity Committee, and Data Committee,
jointly steer local initiatives. The JRC developed a strategic implementation plan of the
Commiission’s digital strategy to align JRC efforts with corporate objectives.
SO1: Digital Culture. The JRC aims to strengthen its digital culture. JRC organizes several
awareness-raising operations and training sessions, in addition to corporate ones. It will introduce
13

an e-learning module and series of live trainings on data management at JRC. The business
planning tool, the JRC Project Browser, requires project leaders to consider the ICT dimension of
every scientific project, ensuring a digital-aware approach from the outset.
SO2: Digital-ready policymaking. Although the JRC is not a policy DG, it remains dedicated to
bolstering digital capabilities for seamless collaboration and information exchange with
policymakers.
SO3: Business-driven digital transformation. The JRC systematically supports business
owners in automating and improving their processes and is committed to advancing data
openness, maturity, and interoperability. Data governance, FAIR (8) principles, and data
management training will be further strengthened. Innovation and AI remain priorities, with the
establishment of the Digital Strategy Office and the implementation of the "AI empowered JRC"
plan.
SO4: Seamless digital environment. JRC is focused on improving its digital landscape
cartography, migrating its scientific activities into a modern and secured ICT environment called
Delta. Governance promotes the reuse of existing systems and increased adoption of cloud
infrastructure services, with a focus on digital sovereignty.
SO5: Green, secure and resilient infrastructure. The JRC will continue promoting a digital
workplace, cybersecurity, and IT greening, including green public procurement criteria and
paperless practices.
Cybersecurity will be reinforced through alignment with the Commission’s Cybersecurity
Strategy 2025–2026, implementation of the Cloud Security Control Baseline that builds on our
active participation in the Cloud Control Management Committee (CCMC), improved vulnerability
management, deployment of Privileged Access Management, secure CI/CD (9) pipelines via
Development, Security, and Operations (DevSecOps), and dedicated training and awareness for a
strong security culture.
Data management
JRC will deploy a data repository and will assess its potential extension as a corporate service in
collaboration with the Directorate-General for Digital Services. In parallel, sovereign data
repositories will be evaluated to enhance the AI readiness of JRC scientific data. The action will
support the move towards a single market of JRC scientific data, increasing compliance with FAIR
principles and enabling data reuse for advanced analytics and AI applications. A report on JRC
data reuse will assess the visibility, uptake and impact of JRC-produced data and propose actions
to enhance their reach and reuse.
Ownership and responsibilities. The JRC will maintain its data governance framework through
the Data Committee and Data Contact Points network, complemented by clearly defined roles of
data owners and data stewards, supported by a central data management service.
Data quality. The JRC will continue to promote the FAIR principles by developing a JRC Data
Quality Dashboard and contributing to central EC tools assessing data FAIRness. It will also
explore the feasibility of a peer review mechanism for JRC datasets prior to publication,
complementing the existing validation process.
Data skills. A mandatory e-learning module on JRC data management will ensure a common
knowledge baseline for new staff, complemented by a targeted training program on data
competencies.
Following the implementation of the JRC Data Strategy, the DG has an established data
governance framework and reached a solid level of maturity across the data management pillars.
(8) Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable
(9) Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment/Continuous Delivery
14

In 2026, targeted actions will be launched to achieve an advanced level in all pillars by 2027,
with the ambition to become a trendsetter in data management by 2029.
The JRC strives to ensure rigorous implementation of personal data protection rules. The JRC
Data Protection Coordinator (DPC) will ensure compliance with Regulation (EU) 2018/1725
advising on data protection records creation and review, data subject requests and breach
assessment. The DPC will work to streamline data protection records procedures with the
Commission’s Data Protection Officer and will provide awareness raising and training on data
protection and AI/Generative AI matters.
For details on the planned outputs please refer to Annex 2, p.26.
C. Sound financial management
Following the GoLive of SUMMA and eProcurement in 2025 a major change management activity
was put in place in the JRC. These change management activities will continue in 2026 including
dedicated training sessions for both financial and operational actors on new developments and
releases of the tools. The JRC’s first level helpdesk will continue to support all JRC practitioners
while dedicated bi-monthly meetings will continue with the actors to exchange best practices and
knowledge. All this support is provided to ensure an efficient and effective management of the
JRCs financial transactions in line with the principle of sound financial management.
As business domain owner of the eProcurement suite, the JRC will continue in its role of providing
strategic direction and value realization to the eProcurement programme ensuring alignment with
the recently adopted 2026-2030 eProcurement Charter. Working collaboratively with the
business process owners, the JRC will drive continuous process improvement and compliance.
The suite aims to be fully integrated, paperless and data-driven, generating efficiency, improving
transparency and user experience, and reinforcing the Commission’s position as a digital leader
in public procurement at the EU institutions. It progressively replaces legacy systems reducing
overlaps and improving efficiency across the EU procurement landscape.
The JRC’s financial, procurement, operational and competitive activity networks will continue to
meet regularly throughout the year to share experiences and best practices across the DG and
to continue to professionalise the JRC’s financial and operational communities aimed at achieving
greater efficiencies and continuously ensuring sound financial management.
Our regular PRI(S)MA (10) newsletters and steering committee meetings will keep JRC
practitioners up to date in 2026 with all the latest changes in tools, templates, guidance etc.
The Public Procurement Advisory Group will continue to perform ex ante checks on the legal and
regulatory aspects of a significant number of JRC procurement procedures. It will give advice to
JRC authorising officers by sub-delegation before award decisions are taken. These control
activities are intended to help mitigate risks that the JRC objectives will not be met.
The “licence to buy” programme, consisting of mandatory and highly recommended training
courses followed by attestation tests will continue to be a prerequisite for the appointment of
new operational actors involved in financial and procurement processes in the JRC.
For details on the planned outputs please refer to Annex 2, p.26.
(10) Procurement information systems management

D. Fraud risk management
The JRC’s updated Action Plan (2025-2027) accompanying its local anti-fraud strategy aims at
mitigating the risks associated with fraudulent activities and promoting a culture of transparency,
accountability, and integrity within the organisation. In line with the Commission's anti-fraud
strategy action plan (11), the JRC is focusing on awareness-raising and the use of IT tools in
preventing and detecting fraud. The JRC’s key outputs for 2026 include the delivery of mandatory
anti-fraud training modules and thematic sessions covering specific topics, including conflict of
interest, authorship, and the implementation of artificial intelligence. A customized anti-fraud
training will be delivered in cooperation with OLAF.
The JRC's dedicated anti-fraud webpage will be updated regularly with the latest news and
developments in the anti-fraud sector. For details on the planned outputs please refer to Annex
2, p.26.
E. Sound environmental management
The JRC remains committed to contributing to the European Commission’s environmental
objectives through the implementation of the EU Eco-Management and Audit Scheme (EMAS)
and the “Greening the Commission” Communication while continuing to perform its core scientific
and policy-support activities of high relevance.
On buildings and working space, and in line with specific objective 8.2 the JRC will: 1) assess
and reduce energy use for scientific activities (e.g. through the completion of MyGreenLab
certification for five laboratories) (12); 2) substitute fossil fuels with renewable energy sources,
including the expansion of photovoltaic capacity in JRC Ispra; 3) renovate and construct
sustainable buildings. On greener mobility and travels, the JRC has already achieved 50%
reduction in CO2 emissions from staff professional travels in 2024 compared to 2019 (13),
maintaining this trend in 2025. The goal for 2026 is to sustain this good performance. To
complement this effort, additional hybrid and electric service vehicles will be introduced. The JRC
will continue promote a circular economy by raising staff awareness on green public
procurement and by integrating its architectural projects into the European framework for
